I loved these films-- The Lady Eve, On the Town, Mr. Smith Goes to Washington-- shout-out to my boy, Jimmy Stewart. I was fascinated by the dramatics, the over-the-top slaps, the sultry looks, the glamorous makeup and hairstyles.

segments.text: And it is shocking, as you'll see, that this is all that's left, because Paul Robeson was so famous. Like, I can't even think of a modern celebrity to match how big he was. segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry

segments.text: For centuries, Russia's labor system of choice was serfdom. Everyone always points out that it's not slavery. segments.text: Russian czars kept this up until around the time of America's Civil War. Then they freed the serfs, who were not slaves, but left them with no resources and forced them to live under Jim Crow-esque restrictions.

But if you read between the lines, she's calling him lazy. She says that she has to constantly chase after him to get him to rehearse and be a professional.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: She says that he is barely interested in Paulie. She calls him a massive flirt who is not cheating on her, but if he did cheat on her, he would never leave her. And Paul is like, I want a divorce right now.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: [AUDIENCE GROANING]

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: After that, there are messy headlines. They kind of spend some time apart. There's this Eat, Pray, Love summer in Paris for Essie.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And then in the movie version of this, so it's all in my head, one day Paul shows back up on the stoop of their flat. He says, Essie, I've made a terrible mistake.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Paul and the sometimes-actress Yolande broke up. Essie says that Yolande chickened out.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So he comes back home, and he and Essie essentially start dating again. In 1933, the two make each other some promises. They will never get divorced or discuss divorce again. They will be together for the rest of their lives. There will never be headlines or gossip about them again. No more Yolandes. They will have an open marriage.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Coming up, Paul and Essie fall in love again, but this time, it's with the Soviet Union. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Emanuele Berry sitting in for Ira Glass. Today's show, "Bless This Mess." Today in our program, we are hearing the story of Paul and Essie Robeson. When we left the couple, the newspapers couldn't stop talking about their unconventional relationship. In part two of our story, all the headlines become about their politics. Here's Nichole and Jason.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So while Paul and Essie were dealing with all their drama, the world around them was changing.

segments.speaker: Benito Mussolini
segments.text: [SPEAKING ITALIAN]

segments.speaker: Chioke I'anson
segments.text: Over in Italy, Benito Mussolini is running the world's first fascist dictatorship. Mussolini invades Ethiopia, forcing the country's emperor into exile.

segments.speaker: Chioke I'anson
segments.text: Ethiopia, the only nation in Africa that hadn't been colonized, is of enormous symbolic importance to the Black diaspora. In response, Black men across America train in hopes of joining the Ethiopian resistance. W.E.B Du Bois and Paul Robeson hold a rally at Madison Square Garden, and 25,000 New Yorkers march through Harlem to show their support for the African nation.

segments.speaker: Chioke I'anson
segments.text: Mussolini's fascist movement spreads. So does Hitler's. America chooses isolationism. The Robesons do not.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Here is how we came to fear the Robesons. All right, so now we're in the mid-1930s. Essie and Paul have remixed their vows. They seem to be doing well. They are splitting their time between London and New York. Now, Paul at this point is so wildly famous. I saw this quote that said that he was as well-known during his lifetime as Abraham Lincoln.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Essie, meanwhile, is still managing Paul, which is just, like, amazing. She's killing it. But she's decided that she's going to go back to school for anthropology. She wants her own outlet. And then Paul gets this invite to go to Moscow. And he and Essie are like, you know what? Let's do it. We've been curious about Russia since way back in the day. Let's go.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: [TRAIN HORN BLARING]

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So the Robesons arrive in Moscow around Christmastime. They received the red carpet treatment. It's all the best this. It's state-of-the-art that. Paul performs Negro spirituals for huge crowds. And you have to picture this.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: He is the son of a slave, singing the plantation songs of his parents to the children of serfs, whose parents had their own versions of plantation songs and similar struggles. So they're listening, and they're vibing. And then he sings the songs again, but in Russian, because he's fluent now. They adore him.

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: [SINGING IN RUSSIAN]

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: The Robesons are part of a whole wave of Black intellectuals that are visiting the USSR at this time, people like Langston Hughes, W.E.B Du Bois, opera singer Marian Anderson. And all of them are saying the same thing. They're like, when we are in the USSR, we are being treated like equals. Which, like, I can't really even imagine what it would have felt like to finally be treated like a human being.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Mm. First of all, it's hard to travel now. Imagine how difficult it was to travel then.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: And then also, I just think, they were creative people. You better get out here and see what's happening. It's good for your imagination. It's good for your creativity. It's good to know that maybe the thumb of oppression might not be as heavy everywhere else, right, and that that's a possibility, that maybe there is freedom at some point. If I could be free here, maybe someday I could be free there.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chioke I'anson
segments.text: The Robesons are getting a very particular experience of the USSR. But the reality is, Stalin, at this point, has perpetrated a genocide in Ukraine. And within two years of the Robeson's visit, Stalin will enact the Great Purge, in which he imprisons or executes his so-called enemies.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: We don't really know how much Essie and Paul knew about Stalin's actions. Maybe they'd heard rumors, but maybe they viewed those rumors as US propaganda.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Obviously, in hindsight, it seems like a clearly controversial thing to have looked past, if they knew anything at all. But what we do know is that after their visit, Paul becomes one of the world's most famous supporters of the USSR. And his son Paulie will later learn that the CIA opened a file on his dad.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Essie, meanwhile, is doing some traveling of her own, inspired by her interest and curiosity about Africa. In 1936, Essie goes to places like South Africa and Uganda, and it kind of radicalizes her.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So she writes this article being like, attention, everyone. Paul and I have traveled essentially Earth at this point, and everywhere we go, we see the same thing, which is workers of every race being exploited.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: After that, she steps away from Paul's world to be a writer and an international speaker on Pan-Africanism, communism, and women's and civil rights. Paulie will later learn that the FBI opened a file on his mom.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: What are you thinking right now?

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Oh, just that the FBI, and the CIA, and the State Department, and all-- just thinking about all the people who had files opened up on them for having an imagination.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: These people are doing nothing other than imagining a better version of the life in which they've been-- the life that has been foisted upon them, you know what I mean-- and trying their best to imagine a space where people who are experiencing similar things might be free and are being punished, or at least being sort of investigated due to said imagination. It's interesting to think about.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So from the 1930s and into the '50s, the two devote themselves to fighting racism, colonialism, and class oppression. Paul becomes one of the leading figures in the Civil and Labor Rights Movement, and he uses his fame and fortune to put on benefit concerts that Black and white people attend.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Paul is organizing against lynching, job discrimination, and mob violence, and he's campaigning for progressive causes around the world.

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: I would just like to add one other word-- that this is a time of struggle.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Paul would speak to packed-out venues-- bars, churches, concert halls, even to kids at summer camp.

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: And that we have to fight against people who are very powerful, people whom it seems are pretty hard to bring down from those top places. But they can be brought down.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: This activism, it doesn't really impact Paul and Essie's popularity. They continue to be stars. But they are called extremists by some. They're told to leave America all the time if they have so many problems with the country.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: But they're like, we're Americans. Our parents built this country. We're going to stay, and we're going to help America realize her promise. This is always their position. But then in 1949, public opinion starts to shift.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So that year, Paul joins a peace conference in Paris, and he gives this speech. And in it, he's basically like, Black and white workers built America. We want to share in its wealth. We're not interested in a war with the USSR.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: The press falsely reports Paul saying Black people would help the Soviet Union in a war against America as revenge for slavery and Jim Crow. This goes viral. Every paper covers it. Public sentiment turns on Paul. The Chicago Defender publishes an article with the headline-- Paul Robeson: Is He a Man or a Soviet Mouse?

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: I'm still a fan. This is what I'm talking about. Yolande would never.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Paul's viral moment, when he was misquoted, has big consequences for him and his family. They're now targets of the US government, and a coordinated effort to discredit and ultimately erase him from every corner of public life begins, which brings me to how we came to forget the Robesons.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: It's 1950. The State Department demands that Paul and Essie sign loyalty oaths disavowing communism. They refuse. Their passports are revoked. So you're Paulie. What are your conversations like with your parents at this point? They're in their 50s, and they're taking on the United States of America.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: I'm proud of my parents.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Mm.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: If I'm me, and they my parents, these the people who raised me, I think I would have been sad, and it would have been-- it would have been anxiety-inducing. But I know-- but I also know that it would have been a waste of my time, a futile endeavor, to try to convince them otherwise.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Right? If them your parents, then you go ahead and you sign up for what it is.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So in 1956, the Robesons get called down to Washington to testify in front of lawmakers. They're going in hopes of getting their passports back.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So now, you have to just remember that this is during the era of the Red Scare. So even though the Robesons, by now, would have learned that the USSR under Stalin is this, like, violent, authoritarian regime, they remain unwavering in their belief in communism.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So Essie's questioned by Joseph McCarthy and his little protege Roy Cohn, who was the mentor to the current president.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: [GAVEL POUNDING]

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: They want to know why she's so obsessed with Africa if she's an American and why she loves it there so much. Essie's like, why is everybody on this committee white? McCarthy's like, because we are who the American people voted for. Are you a Communist?

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And she says, well, Jim Crow is making it very hard for a lot of the American people to vote down South. Maybe if they could, we wouldn't all be here wasting our time.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Paul testifies before the House Un-American Activities Committee. He's asked if he's a Communist, why he loves Stalin so much, why he keeps criticizing America even though he's rich and famous. His contempt for the committee is hilarious. You should absolutely read the transcripts. He's just like, I'm so bored. Why am I here?

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: He reminds them that he's literally a lawyer. If you'll recall, that's where all this started. Plus, he's an orator, and he's a genius. And they're like, obviously we forgot that. Otherwise, we wouldn't have invited all these reporters in here. He's just, like, posing for the reporters. He does not care. They ask him over and over again if he's a Communist, and he says the following.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: "I'm not being tried for whether I am a Communist. I'm being tried for fighting for the rights of my people to be full citizens in this country, and they are not. They are not in Mississippi, and they are not in Alabama. That is why I am here today. You want to shut up every Negro who has the courage to stand up and fight for the rights of his people, for the rights of workers."

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: If you can believe it, after these testimonies, they do not get their passports back.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: I can't believe it.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: I know. I know. I know.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: After the hearings, the Robesons are declared anti-American communists. Paul is labeled the most dangerous man in America by the State Department, and other institutions are like, all right, let's go. And they try to make it so the Robesons never existed, like, literally.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Paul's University, Rutgers, erases any record of his football or sporting career. Newspapers destroy archival materials that mention Paul. The NAACP denounces them. The concert halls that Paul had once filled, they won't book him. He writes a memoir. The mainstream white press refuses to promote or even review it.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: His films and recordings get taken out of circulation. He's blacklisted from the radio, movie screens. And he becomes one of the first artists to be blacklisted from television. He's banned longer than any other performer from this era.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Black churches and unions around the world send their support, but it's not nearly enough to make up for so much lost income. Paul and Essie have to sell their home and move in with Paulie. And all of this is what erasing them from the history books looks like.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: So Paul's actually going to live into the 1970s, but he is hidden from view. And let me just tell you that when I tell white people this next part of the story, they're usually like, what? But as a Black person, I'm like, obviously, because none of this feels unbelievable to a Black person.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: But let's get into it. In 1958, after eight years, the Supreme Court rules that the state can't take your passport over your politics, and the Robesons get theirs back. They relocate to London.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: A couple years later, Paul is in Moscow. He's entertaining in his hotel room, and some uninvited guests arrive. Then Essie, who's back in London, gets a call telling her that Paul is in the hospital.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: She rushes to Paul's side and is told that at some point during or after this party, Paul went into his bathroom and slit his wrists. He was discovered and brought to the hospital experiencing some kind of a mental breakdown, with severe hallucinations and extreme paranoia. The doctors treat him with mild tranquilizers. This seems to help.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Paulie arrives in Moscow. He checks on his dad. Then he grabs a meal. He suddenly begins experiencing some kind of a mental breakdown with severe hallucinations and extreme paranoia.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: After a week, Paulie recovers, but Paul does not. At times, he seems fine, and at other times, he's dangerously depressed and completely disoriented.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And then Paul's London doctor suggests that Essie check him into a clinic called The Priory to receive special treatment. Essie agrees, but after a few months, she finally lets it slip that she's worried about Paul's treatment plan. So Paulie rushes to London, and he's horrified.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: At the clinic, Paul has been subjected to near daily debilitating electroconvulsive therapy and a cocktail of powerful drugs. He's a shell of himself.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Some historians say that maybe he had a mental break. Others wonder if he had bipolar disorder and it appeared in his 60s. They don't like Paulie's theory because he can't produce enough evidence for it, but I'm going to tell you it anyway.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: He says that he finds compelling evidence that the CIA and British intelligence may have conspired to administer LSD and ECT therapy as part of the covert CIA mind control and chemical interrogation research program known as MKUltra.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: I'm obviously a little more toward the Paulie side, where it's like, I think they poisoned him. And for his son to get sick, too?

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Come on, man. We know what it is. Like, I just-- I didn't know that part, and I think that part kind of has me a little emotional and a bit rattled, just because-- I mean, because there's anger there for me.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Yeah, because it's a pattern.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Actually, of Paul, Coretta Scott King will later say, "He was buried alive even before my husband for tapping the same wells of latent militancy." Essie passed away in 1965, and Paul died a decade later. He was 77.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: You know, when I talk about Paul and Essie, it's a little bit painful to tell a story like that as a Black person to another Black person and think about the amount of research that I had to do to know it and that it isn't already known. And I have this feeling. You know, there's this belief that if you do enough, if we do enough, then maybe we can change everything. Maybe we can turn it around or be the change we want to see.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And then I read everything that they did. They did every single thing it feels like a person could think to do to make not only Black life, but all life, better. And we forgot.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And it just makes me-- it makes me sad to know that that's possible. It feels like it should be impossible to erase a legacy of that size, but it wasn't, which means it probably still isn't.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: But that's the thing, right? You say we forgot. We didn't forget. We never knew.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Mm.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Right? The information-- like, his life had been redacted.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Right, that's true.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: And I think-- and this is the thing that I think about all the time, is that if you can't beat me at any of the things, if I am objectively better at all of the things-- my intellectual capacity, my athletic capacity, my creative capacity, my fervor and spirit-- the only thing left to get me is to make it so that I never existed, right-- is to turn me into a ghost.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: The moment that the opportunity arose, he was turned into a ghost. And this is a tricky thing to talk about, because it's one of those-- because it sounds-- it sounds so tinfoil-y.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Yes. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: But if I'm only looking at what is happening, it's like James Baldwin. No, I don't know you hate me, but I know that my-- I know my kids ain't got no books in their schools.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Jason Reynolds
segments.text: Because I don't necessarily think that they're taking these things down because they don't believe them. I think they're taking these things down because they don't want everyone else to believe them. They know exactly who we are.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: You know, when you say they know who we are, people know who we are, I think a lot about the fact that there is something in our ability to disrupt the economic systems of America, the social systems, the political systems. I mean, the whole country had one system that it was built on, which was the enslavement of Black people.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And then it ends, and it has to be overturned. And so they create a new system, where it's like, all right, well, fine, we'll be separate. And then, through our strategy, through our art, through our humanity, through everything that we are, we overturn the social, political, cultural, religious, all these systems again.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And when I'm in archives, when I'm reading the diaries of ancestors, that's the thing that sticks with me. I'm like, oh, this is who we are. We have the power to articulate our lived experience in such a way that people all around the world rise up and say, this is wrong, and join movements and fights for people they've never met, and in a lot of cases, have never even seen.

segments.speaker: Nichole Hill
segments.text: And I think, man, there's so much power in that. And I didn't know, and that is by design.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Nichole Hill-- she's the host of the award-winning show Our Ancestors Were Messy. What you just heard was an adaptation of her original episode. That's right. There is even more Paul and Essie drama. It's a two-parter.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: You can find that episode and more wherever you listen to podcasts, and there are so many wonderful stories that Nichole tells. I highly recommend checking out the episode about Nora Holt and the one about Zora Neale Hurston. Go listen.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: What you're hearing right now is Paul Robeson singing a song he himself wrote to the tune of the "Battle Hymn of the Republic." It was kind of lost to history until a sound designer and editor John DeLore found it last year at a thrift store and gave it to Nichole.

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: (SINGING) From the Bay of Massachusetts out into the Golden Gate,

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: Henry Wallace leads his army 'gainst destruction, fear, and hate

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: We Americans will save the precious land that we create

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: For the people's march is on

segments.speaker: Paul Robeson
segments.text: Glory, glory hallelujah

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Act 2: "Sincerely, Absolutely Not."

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: OK, so you're emancipated from slavery. You resettle in Ohio. Then you get a letter from the man who used to enslave you, asking you to come back and work for him again.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: That is exactly what happened to a man named Jourdon Anderson. Anderson wrote a letter in response. It was published in a newspaper in 1865 and is read here at a live event by Laurence Fishburne.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: To my old master-- the letter. Dayton, Ohio, August 7, 1865.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: To my old master, Colonel P.H. Anderson, Big Spring, Tennessee.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: Sir, I got your letter and was glad to find that you had not forgotten Jourdon and that you wanted me to come back and live with you again, promising to do better for me than anyone else can.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: I have often felt uneasy about you. I thought the Yankees would have hung you before this--

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: --for harboring Rebs that they found at your house. I suppose they never heard about your going to Colonel Martin's to kill the Union soldier that was left by his company in their stable.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: Although you shot at me twice before I left you, I did not want to hear of your being hurt and am glad that you are still living. It would do me good to go back to dear old home again, and see Miss Mary and Miss Martha, Alan, Esther, Green, and Lee. Give my love to them all and tell them I hope we will meet in the better world, if not in this.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: I would have gone back to see you all when I was working in the Nashville Hospital, but one of the neighbors told me that Henry intended to shoot me if he ever got a chance.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: I want to know particularly what the good chance is you propose to give me. I am doing tolerably well here. I get $25 a month, with victuals and clothing, have a comfortable home for Mandy-- hah, the folks call her Mrs. Anderson. And the children, Millie, Jane, and Grundy, go to school and are learning well.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: Now, if you will write and say what wages you will give me, I will better be able to decide whether it would be to my advantage to move back again.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: As to my freedom, which you say I can have, well, there is nothing to be gained on that score, as I got my free papers in 1864 from the Provost Marshal General of the Department of Nashville. Mandy says she would be afraid to go back without some proof that you were disposed to treat us kindly and justly. And we have concluded to test your sincerity by asking you to send us our wages for the time that we served you.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: This will make us forget and forgive old scores and rely on your justice and friendship in the future. I served you faithfully for 32 years and Mandy 20 years. At $25 a month for me, $2 a week for Mandy, our earnings would amount to $11,680. Add this-- the interest for the time of our wages have been kept back, and deduct what you paid for our clothing and three doctor visits for me, pulling a tooth for Mandy, and the balance will show what we are in justice entitled to.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: Please send the money by Adams Express in care of V. Winters, Esquire, Dayton, Ohio. If you fail to pay us for our faithful labors in the past, we can have little faith in your promises in the future. We trust the Good Maker has opened your eyes to the wrongs which you and your fathers have done to me and my fathers in making us toil for you for generations without recompense.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: Here, I draw my wages every Saturday night, but in Tennessee, there was never any payday for the Negroes, any more than for the horses and cows. Surely there will be a day of reckoning for those who defraud the laborer of his hire.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: In answering this letter, please state if there would be any safety for my Millie and Jane, who are now grown up and both good-looking girls. You know how it was with poor Matilda and Catherine. I would rather stay here and starve and die, if it came to that, than to have my girls brought to shame and violence by the wickedness of their young masters.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: You will also please state if there have been any schools open for the colored children in your neighborhood. The great desire of my life now is to give my children an education and have them form virtuous habits.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: Say howdy to George Carter, and thank him for taking the pistol from you when you were shooting at me. Your old servant, Jourdon Anderson.

segments.speaker: Laurence Fishburne
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Laurence Fishburne reading Jordan Anderson's "Letter to my Former Master." What you just heard is a slightly shortened version of the original response. You can find the whole thing and countless other amazing letters on the Letters Live YouTube channel or at their website, letterslive.com. Letters Live is actually coming back to New York City on the 14th. Tickets are on sale now.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: One last little thing to end our show. Recently, I went to the Blacksonian. That is not what it is called. It is called the National Museum of African-American History and Culture. But Blacksonian is more fun.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Anyway, it was a winter morning, busy, full of school children and teachers, parents, and chaperones. I took the escalator down to the bottom floor, to the history galleries, and there, in big white letters against a black wall, it says "Slavery and Freedom, 1400 to 1877," and then this short caption.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: "500 years ago, a new form of slavery transformed Africa, Europe, and the Americas. For the first time, people saw other human beings as commodities, things to be bought, sold, and exploited to make enormous profits. This system changed the world. The United States was created in this context, forged by slavery."

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I stopped reading there-- forged by slavery. And my first thought was, how are they allowed to say this? Like, why hasn't this been flagged?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And then, my next thought was, what a fucked up thought. I know the US does not exist without slavery, but it wasn't about what I knew to be true, but what's allowed to be true in this country right now. And it freaked me out, because what the hell, Emanuele? But there was also something comforting about recognizing what my brain was doing.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The way history is being reshaped in this moment, it's about power. It's about how the United States is changing. I think I've read the phrase "sliding towards authoritarianism" countless times this year.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: But it's not a slide, is it? It's more like steps-- steps we the people are taking-- not just politicians, all of us. We're changing, too, taking steps so small you can miss them. But here in this museum, I caught my foot mid-air.
